summaries.Foundations: Genes can influence the likelihood of traits without guaranteeing them. Neurons communicate using chemical messengers at synapses. The central nervous system contains the brain and spinal cord. Endocrine glands release hormones; the hypothalamus helps regulate endocrine activity.
summaries.Brain & sleep: The cerebral cortex is the folded outer layer of the cerebrum. The hemispheres generally receive information from, and control movement on, opposite sides of the body. Circadian rhythms follow an approximately 24-hour pattern. REM combines rapid eye movements with active brain activity and normally reduced skeletal muscle tone.
summaries.Sensation: Transduction converts sensory energy into neural signals. Trichromatic theory concerns three cone types; opponent processing concerns opposing color channels. Place theory links pitch to the location of activity along the cochlea. Conductive hearing loss concerns sound transmission; sensorineural loss concerns inner-ear or auditory-nerve damage. Gate control concerns modulation of pain signals. Taste receptor cells occur in taste buds, many of which are in tongue papillae.
summaries.Neurotransmitters: Learn the eight messengers in the supplied table by function, then compare the pairs that are easy to confuse. Disease links in the screenshot are study associations, not one-chemical explanations of disorders. The GABA problem cell is unclear and is not assessed; its inhibitory function is assessed.
summaries.Nervous system: The CNS contains the brain and spinal cord; the PNS includes nerves outside them. The PNS divides into somatic and autonomic systems. Somatic pathways control skeletal muscles; autonomic pathways regulate internal organs and glands. Sympathetic activity supports fight-or-flight responses, while parasympathetic activity supports rest and digestion. Sensory (afferent) neurons carry signals toward the CNS, motor (efferent) neurons carry them away, and interneurons connect neurons within the CNS. Glia support neurons; Schwann cells form myelin around PNS axons and aid repair. A withdrawal reflex can be integrated in the spinal cord before conscious awareness.

terms.Dopamine: Motor movement and alertness. Low activity is associated with Parkinson’s disease; excess dopamine activity in some pathways is associated with schizophrenia.
terms.Serotonin: Mood regulation. The screenshot associates low serotonin with depression; this is a simplified association, not a complete causal explanation.
terms.Norepinephrine: Alertness and arousal. The screenshot associates low norepinephrine with depression; a disorder cannot be inferred from one messenger level.
terms.Glutamate: Excitation and memory. The screenshot links glutamate with migraines and seizures. Do not treat normal glutamate signaling as harmful.
terms.GABA: Inhibition. GABA is a major inhibitory neurotransmitter. The screenshot’s problem cell is unclear and is not used as an answer key.
terms.Endorphins: Pain control. The screenshot associates endorphins with addiction. Learn pain modulation as the core function.
terms.Substance P: Pain perception. The screenshot associates reduced substance P with reduced pain perception.
terms.Acetylcholine: Motor movement. The screenshot links reduced acetylcholine with Alzheimer’s disease and also notes myasthenia gravis and muscle weakness.
terms.Genetic predisposition: Inherited factors that increase likelihood without guaranteeing an outcome.
terms.Hypothalamus: Brain structure that helps regulate endocrine activity.
terms.Cerebral cortex: Folded outer layer of the cerebrum.
terms.Hemispheres: Left and right halves of the cerebrum.
terms.Transduction: Conversion of sensory energy into neural signals.
terms.Thalamus: A major sensory relay; smell is an exception to the usual initial relay.
terms.Trichromatic theory: Color vision begins with three cone types, often described as red-, green-, and blue-sensitive.
terms.Opponent-process theory: Opposing color channels: red–green, blue–yellow, black–white.
terms.Place theory: Pitch relates to location of strongest cochlear response.
terms.Sensorineural hearing loss: Damage involving the inner ear or auditory nerve.
terms.Gate control theory: Pain transmission is modulated by neural gating.
terms.Papillae: Tongue bumps that can contain taste buds.
terms.PNS: Peripheral nervous system: nerves outside the brain and spinal cord.
terms.Somatic nervous system: PNS division involved in voluntary skeletal-muscle control.
terms.Autonomic nervous system: PNS division regulating internal organs and glands.
terms.Sympathetic nervous system: Autonomic branch supporting fight or flight.
terms.Parasympathetic nervous system: Autonomic branch supporting rest and digestion.
terms.Glial cells: Cells that support, nourish, protect, and maintain neurons.
terms.Schwann cells: PNS glia that form myelin and aid axon repair.
terms.Sensory (afferent) neurons: Carry sensory input toward the CNS.
terms.Motor (efferent) neurons: Carry output away from the CNS to effectors.
terms.Effector: A muscle or gland responding to motor output.
terms.Withdrawal reflex: A rapid protective response that can be integrated in the spinal cord.
